Revised assessment incorporating SLOOS: The intermeeting 50 bp cut (to 1.00–1.25%), lower IOER (1.10%), and continued T-bill purchases/repo operations are decisively accommodative and aimed at preempting downside risks and safeguarding money market functioning. However, the latest SLOOS points to headwinds on the credit-supply side that could blunt transmission. Banks reported tighter standards and other terms on C&I loans and construction/land development loans, raised credit score thresholds and reduced credit limits, and saw weaker demand for construction/land development loans. Looking ahead to 2020, banks expected tighter lending standards, reduced risk tolerance, and deterioration in loan portfolios, collateral values, and some consumer segments (e.g., HELOCs), with performance concerns for loans to small firms and syndicated non‑leveraged loans. While some consumer loan standards and demand were reported as unchanged, the overall SLOOS bias is toward tightening. Combined with the FSR’s note of elevated vulnerabilities despite solid bank capital/liquidity, this suggests the Fed’s easing will cushion but not fully offset tightening private credit channels amid the evolving COVID-19 shock. Net effect: more negative near-term outlook than previously assessed.
